text: The assembly will now hear an address by
his excellency Muhammad Van Ali,
President of the Cooperative Republic of
Guyana.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
I extend my congratulations
on your election as president of the
81st session of the General Assembly. I
wish you every success as you undertake
this important responsibility
at a moment when multilateralism and
indeed the United Nations faces profound
challenges.
I also express my sincere appreciation
to your predecessor for her stewardship
over the past year.
I take this opportunity to record
Guyana's gratitude to the Secretary
General, his excellency Antonio Gutterz
for his distinguished service to the
United Nations and to the cause of
humanity. His place in the history of
this institution is assured not mereily
by the office he has occupied
but by the principles he has steadfastly
upheld. The courage and profoundity with
which he has spoken when silence would
have been easier. and his rare ability
to hold before the world a clear mirror
of the perils that confront our age and
the possibilities that still beckon
beyond them. Mr. President,
one year ago, I stood at this very
podium and reminded this assembly that
if the United Nations is to remain
humanity's shest hope for a just and
peaceful world, it must have the courage
to confront aggression and the well and
the will to engage fully with the
defining question of our age. I also
argued that we must be bold enough to
undertake the institutional reforms
necessary to strengthen the
organization,
enhance its credibility and enable it to
meet the challenges of a changing world.
Indeed, I am pleased that the theme of
this year assembly, and I quote,
restoring trust, managing
transformation, a United Nations that
delivers for all, end of quote,
acknowledges the need for this
organization to be fit for purpose, to
respond to the challenges, and to seize
the possibilities of our time. Today we
confront a climate catastrophe and
energy crisis, food insecurity,
biodiversity loss, armed conflicts, and
geopolitical tensions. The horror of
genocide, a spiraling cost of living
crisis, a mountain death crisis,
widening inequalities within and among
nations, and perhaps most troubling of
all, a weakening of multilateralism
itself.
Yet if history has taught us anything,
it is that when it is that even when the
world seemed to stand at the precipice,
humanity has never been entirely without
the means to draw it back from the
brink. We have ended wars that seem
without end. We have confronted economic
calamities that threatened the
foundations of societies. We have
overcome dangers that presented
existential threats. Time and again, it
has been our inventiveness, our courage,
and above all, our willingness to act
together that have opened the path where
none seemed to exist.
This is why I do not wish to linger or
lament further upon the difficulties
before us. I wish instead to turn our
gaze toward the possibilities that lie
beyond them. For within every crisis
lies a summons to solutions. Within
every disruption and opportunity for
renewal and within every uncertainty the
possibility of shaping a better future.
The possibility before us are immense.
We have the possibility of silencing the
guns through dialogue and diplomacy.
The world does not need more
sophisticated instruments of
destruction. It needs a more
sophisticated capacity for peace. In
this regard, I reiterate Guyana's call
for a just and lasting solution to the
crisis in the Middle East. One that
brings an end to the suffering of
innocent civilians and recognizes the
Palestinian people's legitimate right to
self-determination
and to secure homeland of their own.
Reiterate our support for a two-state
solution.
We call as well for an end to the Russia
Ukraine war and the war in Sudan and for
peaceful resolution of all conflicts
that continue to consume lives, uproot
families and extinguish the hopes of
millions in other parts of our world.
We reiterate our call for a viable
solution for Cuba, one that is peaceful,
people centered, development focused,
and allows for the full aspiration of
the Cuban people to be realized. Guy
reiterates Cariccom's offer to play a
meaningful role in achieving this
objective
in Haiti. re re resolving the
multi-dimensional challenges remains
central to achieving democracy,
stability, peace, and prosperity for the
Haitian people. The sustained support of
the international community through the
provision of key financial and material
resources is critical to realizing these
objectives. Ultimately, the future of
Haiti must be Haitianled and Haitian
owned. Mr. President, turning to my own
country, Guyana's always advanced the
peaceful settlement of the controversy
in relation to our border with
Venezuela.
Despite the historical truth clearly
outlined in the arbitral award of 1899
that determined the full perfect and
final settlement of our border with
Venezuela, we endured long and repeated
provocations and aggression. The matter
was referred to the international court
of justice by the secretary general
acting pursuant to the Geneva agreement
and the court twice pronounced on his
jurisdiction to hear the matter.
Recourse to the ICJ came after decades
of efforts to resolve the controversy
bilaterally, including through a mixed
commission and the good offices of the
UN Secretary General. In full respect
for international law, Guyana
participated and encouraged Venezuela to
participate in the proceedings of the
ICJ.
Now that we have both participated in
the hearings which were completed in May
we urge Venezuela to abide by the
forthcoming ruling in accordance with
obl their obligation under the UN
charter as Guyana will do.
We look forward to a new era of
neighborly relations in the interests of
our peoples, the development of our
countries, and the stability and
prosperity of our region. Mr. President,
in pursuit of a stronger and safer
region, Guyana is honored to be a
founding member of the Shield of the
Americas, launched by President Trump in
March 2026.
Since the founding of this initiative,
Guyana has worked closely with the
United States and 13 other like-minded
nations that believe in building a
western hemisphere that values freedom,
peace, economic prosperity, and a shared
responsibility and commitment to
fighting transnational crime and
criminal networks. It is it is our
collective responsibility to never allow
our region to be overtaken by gangs or
criminal networks. We understand that is
it that is that it is only through
partnership, shared intelligence and
cooperation that we can effectively
tackle the threats they pose to our
economies and the livelihoods of our
citizens. This week, I am pleased to
join members of the Shield of Americas
in adopting a joint communicate which
underscores our collective resolve to
strengthen the resilience of our region
in economic security and multilateral
coordination.
Mr. President, we stand at the threshold
of a new era of technological
advancement. Artificial intelligence,
biotechnology,
digital communications, and other
extraordinary breakthroughs offer the
prospect of transforming health,
education, agriculture, productivity,
and public services on a scale scarcely
imaginable a generation ago.
But a true measure of technological
progress will not be how powerful our
machines become, but how much more
empowered our people become. Technology
must not become the privilege of the
few. It must become the servant of all
humanity.
Mr. President,
we have before us a new opportunity for
sustainable development. Development
must not merely make our economies
richer. It must make our societies
better. We must not allow for the
slippage in our pursuit of the
sustainable development goals. We must
renew our commitment to them not as an
inventory of promises but as a covenant
with our people's and practical
blueprint for ensuring the development
reaches every citizen. protects
generations yet unborn and creates
lasting inclusive prosperity.
One way to arrest the slippage is as
Guyana is doing to mainstream the goals
into our national development
strategies, public policies and budgets
so that they become embedded in the
priorities we set and the resources we
commit rather than remaining
aspirations. The SDGs must not only
guide our ambitions, they must shape our
choices and our national priorities. In
Guyana,
we have made significant advances,
including universal health care, free
education, modern infrastructure,
accelerated access to affordable
housing, opportunities for full
employment, acceleration of financing
for small and medium-siz enterprises,
and digitizing service delivery. Mr.
President, two years ago at this very
podium, I committed Guyana to provide
global leadership on biodiversity.
In July 2025, under Guyana's leadership,
the Global Biodiversity Alliance was
established as an inclusive platform. In
just one year, the alliance expanded
from 17 to 138 members, bringing
together governments, institutional
organization,
including the UN, development banks,
indigenous peoples, local communities,
scientists, universities, and the
private sector. The second conference of
the of the alliance to be held in
October 2026
will begin to mobilize the resources and
partnerships to deliver its ambitions.
At the same time, we continue to advance
our lowcarbon development strategy
focused on turning forest stewardship
and climate action into a new model for
sustainable development. Mr. President,
as we commence this 81st session, we
have the opportunity to build a United
Nations that is truly fit for purpose.
The crisis confronting multilateralism
can become the catalyst for its renewal.
The United Nations must not be a
monument to the past. It must become an
instrument for the future. We need a
security council that reflects the
geopolitical realities of the 21st
century, not the power structures of
A council that embraces the emerg the
emerging multipolarity of our world,
including permanent representation from
Africa and Latin America and the
Caribbean.
Mr. Mr. President, if the United Nation
is to remain humanity's best hope, then
this is not the hour to retreat from
multilateralism.
This is the hour to reclaim and to renew
it. For it is in times such as these,
when wars rage across borders, when the
shadow of existential threats falls
across the future of human civilization,
when the old certinities are dissolving
before our eyes, that multilateralism
must rise. Multilateralism
rests upon the proposition that our
destinies are bound together. That the
security of one, the security of one
cannot be at the insecurity of another.
And that in an interependent world,
cooperation is a necessity. and where
there can be no enduring prosperity when
inequality depend deepens and no just
international order when rules are
applied selectively.
It is to that truth that this 81st
session of the general assembly must
recommit itself. But recommmitment
cannot mean merely repeating the
language of yesterday. The world has
changed and multilateralism
must change with it. We need a new and
invigorated multilateralism.
One equal to the turbulence of our age.
Sufficiently courageous
to confront its trials, sufficiently
imaginative
to navigate its transformations,
and sufficiently principled to defend
the rule of international law.
To make the United Nations fit for
purpose, we must make it more
transparent, accountable, and
responsive. We must strengthen the
General Assembly and give great and give
greater weight to its deliberative and
representative authority. We must bring
greater coherence to a system too often
divided by institutional rivalries,
bureaucratic silos, and competing
mandates. We must ensure that the
resources of the UN match the
responsibilities we have entrusted to
it.
But institutions do not reform
themselves.
They require leadership capable of
seeing beyond the present
and imagining the institutions
the future demands.
The United Nations needs leadership that
can bring its different organs,
agencies, and programs into greater
unity of purpose. Leadership that can
build bridges where division has become
habitual. Leadership that can defend the
principles of the charter without fear
or favor. The United Nations needs its
next general secretary to work with all
member states to restore confidence in
the organization, mobilize its energies
and turn the language of multilateralism
from aspiration into action. The reform
of the United Nations, the restoration
of trust and the need to manage
transformation is therefore inseparable
from the question of leadership. And the
choice of its next secretary general
will be in no small measure a choice
about the kind of United Nations we wish
to leave to the generations that follow.
It is in this spirit that Guyana has put
forward the candidature of our
excellency Carlin Rodrig Burke
for the office of secretary general of
the United Nations. She has served her
country,
represented the developing world, and
worked within the multilateral system
with a deep understanding of both its
promise and its imperfections.
We believe that her experience, her
convictions, her record of service speak
directly to the kind of leadership this
moment demands. Her candidature
therefore requires special significance
amid the profound challenges confronting
the United Nations and its national
order. We need leadership capable of
restoring trust without compromising
principles, of listening without
surrendering conviction, of building
bridges across the widening chasms
between north and south, between large
states and small, between the developed
and developing worlds. We need a
secretary general who will defend the
charter not only when it is politically
convenient but precisely when its
principles are under pressure. On a
personal note, Mr. President
Carolyn Rodrig Burket

cross every struggle,

an indigenous woman

defining every challenge and rising to

Her character

Her accomplishments

This is an individual
of extreme qualities.
Not because she's a gy,
not because she come from Guyana,
but because I know personally and many
of you know this too. The permanent
representatives sitting here in New
York. You know her character.
You know her integrity. You know her
will. You know her commitment. You know
her love for humanity. You know her love
for this world.
And I know that this world will be a
better place with Carlin Rodrig as the
Secretary General of the United Nations.
In the humblest of ways, I call on the
P5, the Security Council, and every
member and every member here
to look beyond the small country that
nominated her.
Look beyond the small country that
nominated her. Caricom as a body has
endorsed her
and let us rise to the challenge of
giving this indigenous woman the chance
of helping us craft together the United
Nations we want to see succeed.
The responsibility for recommending the
next secretary general rests in the
forest instance with the security
council and we therefore respectfully
place before its members
the candidature of Carllin Rodrig Burke
endorsed by the Caribbean community. We
invite all to consider her candidacy on
its merits and to judge whether her
vision, experience, expertise, and
record can help restore confidence in
the United Nations at this critical
moment. Mr. President, the United
Nations was conceived in hope and that
hope remains alive in the pursuit of
peace, security, and human progress over
the perpetuation
of division and war. This is why we must
not abandon multilateralism
because it is imperfect. We must renew
it because humanity still needs it.
Let us therefore build a United Nations
that does not merely reflect the world
as it is, but help create the world as
it ought to be. A world where law
restrains power, cooperation overcomes
division, and every human being can look
to the future with hope. Guyana believes
that the choice remains ours as to
whether the divisions of our age will
define the future or whether nations can
summon the will to build a more
peaceful, secure, and prosperous
international order. The United Nations
must be at the heart of that endeavor.
Not as an institution looking back at
the world it was created to serve, but
as one helping humanity shape the world
that is yet to come. May God bless all
of you. May God bless our humanity. May
God guide us to peace and keep our world
safe, our children safe, and give us all
the where it all to build nations that
are prosperous. I thank you and God
bless you.
